extracted.intended_audience: researchers, bibliometricians, research funders and policymakers interested in scientometrics/impact prediction
extracted.subtask_description: Developing models to forecast publications' long-term citation impact by combining early citations, readership metrics (e.g., Mendeley), and non-scientific predictors such as journal metrics, authorship and reference-list characteristics, funding, and open-access status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early citation counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate early citation counts as predictors of a publication's long-term citation impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper states that early citations are a significant predictor of long-term impact; traditional citation-based models that rely solely on early citations often fall short, but early citations remain an important component of improved predictive models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mendeley readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Include Mendeley readership (early readership measures) as an input feature when forecasting long-term impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mendeley readership is reported as a significant predictor alongside early citations and improves prediction accuracy when integrated into models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal impact factor (JIF)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use journal-level impact metrics (e.g., journal impact factor) as non-scientific predictors of long-term citation outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal impact factor contributes additional predictive power beyond early citations and readership, and should be included among non-citation predictors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship characteristics (including authorship diversity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model features of authorship (such as number/diversity of authors) as predictors of future citation impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorship diversity is identified as providing additional contribution to prediction; authorship-related features should be considered in the predictor set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference list characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate characteristics of a paper's reference list (e.g., length, recency, cited sources) into prediction models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference list characteristics are mentioned as non-scientific factors that can influence long-term impact and should be included as explanatory variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding status
rubrics_metrics.description: Use information on whether a publication was funded as a predictor variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding has predictive power primarily in the short term; the study finds funding's contribution diminishes over time, so treat its temporal effect accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-access status
rubrics_metrics.description: Include open-access (OA) status as a predictor of long-term citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open-access status shows predictive power that diminishes over time (influence is primarily short-term), so models should account for temporal decay of OA effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate early citations, readerships, and non-scientific factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine early citation counts and readership metrics with non-scientific predictors (journal metrics, authorship/reference features, funding, OA) rather than relying on a single type of indicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper's central claim: integrating non-citation-based factors with early citations captures a more complex view of scholarly impact and outperforms models that rely only on early citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use regression models to evaluate predictor effects over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ regression modelling (and related statistical approaches) to quantify the contribution of each predictor to long-term impact and to track how predictive power changes over different time horizons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study developed regression models on a Web of Science dataset to evaluate predictors' impact over time; practitioners should similarly model temporal dynamics and report how effects change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal dynamics and diminishing effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for temporal dynamics: some predictors (e.g., OA, funding) have strong short-term effects that diminish, whereas others (early citations, readership) maintain predictive significance longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models should not treat predictor effects as static; include time-varying analyses or interaction terms with time to capture diminishing or evolving predictive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset selection and scope (Web of Science, national sample example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a representative bibliographic dataset (the paper uses Italian-authored publications from the Web of Science) to train and test prediction models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of dataset influences generalizability; the paper's approach used a national sample from Web of Science—future applications should consider dataset coverage, discipline mix, and geographic scope when evaluating model performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend models with broader altmetrics and cross-disciplinary validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Broaden predictor sets to include other altmetrics beyond Mendeley and validate models across disciplines and regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors recommend future research to incorporate broader altmetrics and expand applications to other disciplines and regions to improve generalizability and robustness.
